claims.text: A coupled DFT and machine-learning atomistic approach can separately quantify lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will predict thermal conductivity with an error margin of ±20%, compared with ±50% for earlier methods.
The target material states are near-pristine crystalline HfNbTaTiZr and a variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Direct ab initio phonon calculations avoid reliance on a Debye-temperature approximation.
Atomistic simulation with Monte Carlo sampling can incorporate vacancies, interstitials, and oxygen impurities into high-temperature HfNbTaTiZr configurations.
The approach is applicable from 50 to 1200 K, using near-pristine configurations at 50–300 K and defect- or impurity-containing configurations at 300–1200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Defect distributions and impurity incorporation mediate phonon scattering and electron scattering in ways that permit the two transport channels to be separated.
Calculating phonon dispersions and independently simulating electron-scattering events will disentangle lattice and electronic heat transport.
Accounting for atomic-scale defects and impurities will improve thermal-conductivity accuracy relative to Debye-based and ideal-crystal approximations.
For the oxygen-containing sample at high temperature, the predicted total conductivity will fall near the measured range of 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier predictive methods typically used Debye approximations or perfect bulk-crystal simulations.
Earlier methods conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
Earlier methods had thermal-conductivity error margins of approximately ±50%.
Predictions outside 50–1200 K or for extremely disordered microstructures may fail because of unmodeled effects such as phase instability.
The electron-scattering contribution below 200 K and the effects of heterogeneous defect distributions at high temperature remain quantitatively uncertain.
Lattice and electronic conductivity contributions can be independently measured using thermal Hall or modulation methods over the proposed ranges.
A total-conductivity deviation greater than ±20%, or disagreement with independently measured lattice and electronic components, will falsify the hypothesis.
